title: Into the pit (Genesis 37:12–36)
hookLine: his brothers throw him in a pit and sell him for twenty pieces of silver
carry: the pit is not the end

cards: Jacob sends Joseph on an errand: go see if your brothers are all right, and bring me word. They're far from home with the flocks, a long walk north. Joseph gets lost, and a stranger has to point the way.
Picture the brothers on a hillside, squinting at a figure in the distance. They know him from a long way off; maybe it's the coat. One of them says, here comes the dreamer.
Before he even reaches them, they've decided what to do.

teach.h: KILL HIM, OR THROW HIM IN?
teach.b: Their first plan is murder: kill him, throw him in a pit, say a wild animal ate him, and see what becomes of his dreams.
Reuben, the oldest, talks them out of it: throw him in alive, he says, secretly planning to come back and rescue him.
So they strip off the coat and throw him in. In the King James Bible: "the pit was empty, there was no water in it." A dry cistern.
Then the brothers sit down to eat. Joseph is in the hole, and they have lunch. Years later they'll remember hearing him plead.
A caravan of traders comes by on its way to Egypt, and Judah asks: what profit is there in killing our brother? Let's sell him.

So they sell him for twenty pieces of silver. Genesis names the buyers as Ishmaelites and also as Midianites, and readers still puzzle over how the two fit. Reuben comes back, finds the pit empty, and tears his clothes.

teach.h: A COAT DIPPED IN GOAT'S BLOOD.
teach.b: The brothers dip the coat in a goat's blood and bring it to Jacob. The man who once wore goat skins to fool his blind father is fooled by a goat.
He says an evil beast has devoured Joseph, and refuses to be comforted: I will go down to the grave mourning.

teach.h: THE PIT WAS EMPTY, THERE WAS NO WATER IN IT.
teach.b: And the last line: Joseph is sold in Egypt, to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh. He is alive. The pit was not the end.
Some Christian readers hear an early echo of Jesus, betrayed by those close to him for pieces of silver.

how: Christian tradition has often read Joseph's betrayal as a foreshadowing of Jesus, betrayed for silver, and the story is used in teaching about families torn apart by envy.

games.q: you're Judah. your brother is in a dry pit, and some of the others still talk of killing him. a caravan bound for Egypt passes. what do you do?
o: pull him out and take him home.
say: don't kill him, sell him to the traders.
walk away and leave it to the others.
games.why: Judah says: what profit is it if we slay our brother? they sell him for twenty pieces of silver. Judah's story isn't over: he'll stand in this same kind of choice again.

practice: Hold in mind someone hurt by the people who were supposed to protect them; maybe someone you know, maybe you. Without reliving the details, picture them at the bottom of the pit, and picture a way out, even if you can't see it yet.
If you pray, you can pray for them by name; if you don't, hold them with care.

wordCard.voice: Bor. Hebrew for a pit or cistern: where Joseph's brothers threw him before selling him to traders bound for Egypt.

orig.note: Hebrew: a pit or cistern dug in the ground. later Joseph uses the same word for the prison in Egypt.

carryVoice: Your line: the pit is not the end. Joseph was alive, and the story kept going. Day three hundred sixty-seven, done.
